title: Short Stuff: Smelly Homes
summary: Short Stuff episode on why homes smell and what to do about it. Josh opens with a joke about his fear that his house smells, then tells a story about friends' Los Angeles-area houses all sharing the same distinctive "house smell." Chuck and Josh explain sensory adaptation (olfactory desensitization): people stop noticing their own home's odors within minutes, so those with smelly houses often don't know. Chuck admits his house has four-plus pets and a dog couch. Tips include removing mildewed towels, cleaning litter boxes, checking filters and mold, using dried lavender or eucalyptus, and citrus. They discuss Febreze's history: early ads targeting smoky bars failed, and the campaign shifted to positioning it as a final step in cleaning. They explain that Febreze traps odor molecules in beta-cyclodextrin rings. They discuss "fragrance" labeling loopholes that can hide thousands of chemicals and a 2009 Environmental Working Group study of air fresheners. Chuck plugs his wife Emily's company, Mama Bath and Body (lovemamabathandbody), which makes soy candles with cotton wicks and room spray. The episode closes with a critique of federal regulation of fragrance products.

segments.title: Intro and the friends' houses that smell the same
segments.summary: Josh introduces the fear of a smelly house and tells a story about several Los Angeles-area friends' houses sharing the same distinctive house smell, which he can't describe.

segments.title: Sensory adaptation and why you can't smell your own home
segments.summary: The hosts explain that people become desensitized to their home's odors within a few breaths and after about a week away, so people with smelly homes often don't notice. Chuck says his household with multiple pets must smell, and Josh reassures him.

segments.title: Low hanging fruit: cleaning up smell sources
segments.summary: Tips for removing home odors: get rid of mildewed towels, keep litter boxes clean, keep ducts and filters clean, and address mold and mildew.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before discussing ways to make a house smell good.

segments.title: Natural scents and HVAC distribution
segments.summary: Suggestions for natural home fragrance such as dried lavender or eucalyptus, placed in the return air duct so the scent circulates through the HVAC system. Chuck mentions using a lemon squeeze on a filter for a brief citrus scent.

segments.title: Febreze's marketing history and how it works
segments.summary: Febreze's early ads targeting smoky bars and couches failed because people who needed it didn't realize their homes smelled. The campaign shifted to positioning it as the final step of cleaning. Febreze uses beta-cyclodextrin, a donut-shaped carbohydrate that traps odor molecules so they can't bind to smell receptors.

segments.title: Fragrance labeling and the Environmental Working Group study
segments.summary: US law lets companies list thousands of chemicals under the label fragrance. The Environmental Working Group found Febreze had more chemicals than listed, some toxic, in a 2009 study; the hosts note changes may have occurred since. Gel toilet and plug-in air fresheners were called the bigger offenders.

segments.title: Mama Bath and Body plug
segments.summary: Chuck promotes his wife Emily's company, Mama Bath and Body, which makes room spray with water, alcohol, and essential oils and soy candles with cotton wicks.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts criticize federal regulation of fragrance products and sign off.
